vignette:
Rajesh's Story

Rajesh was sixty-four when he first sat in a therapist's office, though the man who arrived that Tuesday morning seemed older. His hands trembled slightly as he gripped the armrest of the chair, and his eyes carried the exhausted wariness of someone who had not slept properly in months. Thirty-two years ago, in the summer of 1992, Rajesh had been working as a junior supervisor at a textile factory in Gujarat when three men forced him into a locked storage room at gunpoint. They held him there for eighteen hours-a deliberate, methodical captivity. He was bound to a chair in near-total darkness, with only the sound of his own breathing and the occasional scrape of movement in the shadows. The men had threatened him, demanded money the factory did not have, and left him alone for long stretches, returning unpredictably to reinforce their threats. The worst part, Rajesh had come to understand over three decades, was that he had been utterly powerless. He could not negotiate, could not run, could not protect himself. When police finally breached the room at 2:47 in the morning-a time burned into his memory-he had wept with a relief so profound it had terrified him.

He had rebuilt his life after that. He immigrated to America in 1995, married Priya, worked steadily as a warehouse manager, raised two children who were now adults with lives of their own. For years, the memory had faded into the background, manageable, almost dormant. Then, about eight months ago, something shifted. It began with the evenings. At 2:47 p.m.-that exact hour-Rajesh would feel a tightness in his chest. His palms would sweat. He would find himself unable to focus on work, and by the time that time of day arrived, he had begun leaving the warehouse early, making excuses to his supervisor. When that time approached, he would leave before it could catch him-better to slip away than to sit at his desk and feel his body betray him. The moment he felt the first flutter of panic, he would seek out Priya or check his phone obsessively, anything to interrupt the sensation, to convince himself that this time nothing bad would happen. The timing was so specific that it felt almost supernatural, as though his body remembered what his mind had tried to forget. Alongside this, any mention of snakes-a photograph in a magazine, a news story about a cobra sighting, even a casual reference in conversation-would send him spiraling. When 2:47 p.m. approached, he would leave the warehouse early, making excuses to his supervisor-better to slip away than to sit at his desk and feel his body betray him. The moment a snake appeared in conversation or image, he would seek out Priya or check his phone obsessively, anything to interrupt the sensation and convince himself that this time nothing bad would happen. In the storage room, there had been a snake. He had not seen it clearly in the darkness, but he had heard it, felt it brush past his leg in the suffocating black. It had never bitten him, but the possibility had been its own torture. Now, decades later, the mere word "snake" could trigger a cascade of dread.

The worst trigger, though, was nighttime. As darkness fell, Rajesh's body would tense. Bedtime became something he dreaded with an intensity that baffled even him. He began staying awake as long as possible, sitting in the living room with lights blazing, watching television with the volume low so as not to wake Priya. Each night when darkness came, he would flood the bedroom with light and ask Priya again for reassurance, and when that failed to hold, he would run his hands over his skin, checking, always checking, as though the ritual could keep the night from swallowing him whole. When sleep finally overtook him, he would wake in the dark and panic, his heart racing, convinced that he was back in that room. To manage this, he had taken to sleeping with every light in the bedroom on, and he had asked Priya, again and again, to reassure him that he was safe, that nothing bad would happen to him during the night. She would tell him what he needed to hear, but within an hour, the reassurance would dissolve, and he would ask again. He had also begun checking his body obsessively-running his hands over his arms and legs, inspecting his skin for marks or injuries, as though the act of looking could prevent something terrible from occurring. These rituals gave him a few moments of temporary calm, but they never lasted. Each night, the cycle would restart.

What had begun to terrify Rajesh most was the conviction that he could not stop bad things from happening. He had been powerless in that room, and he had come to believe that powerlessness was his permanent condition. Having settled into the certainty that he could not prevent harm, he walked into each evening already braced for catastrophe-the threat arrived with him before darkness had even fully fallen. His body moved through the warehouse, through his home, through conversations with the weight of that belief pressing down: nothing he did would matter, danger was always closing in. Bad things simply happened to him, and there was nothing he could do to prevent them. This thought had begun to poison other areas of his life. He wondered, with increasing frequency, whether his life was even worth living anymore-whether the constant vigilance, the sleeplessness, the relentless checking and reassurance-seeking was simply prolonging an existence that had lost its meaning. The more he sought reassurance, the more he seemed to need it. The more he checked his body, the more convinced he became that something was wrong. The avoidance of sleep only made him more anxious about nighttime, which made him avoid it more intensely. His safety behaviours had drawn a map of dread around his own home: the lights that could never be turned off, the reassurances that never quite held, the body he could never quite trust-each one a daily acknowledgement that nighttime itself was a threat he could not escape. At work, his performance had deteriorated. He had called in sick seventeen times in the past four months. His supervisor had begun to question his reliability, and Rajesh had felt the sting of that judgment-another confirmation, in his mind, that he was failing, that he could not control what was happening to him.

During the day, he had developed another habit: he would frequently glance behind him, checking to see if someone was following, if some threat was closing in. At the warehouse, where he had once moved with confident authority, he now felt exposed and hunted. His coworkers had noticed the change. They did not understand why he seemed so on edge, why he would suddenly turn around as though startled, why he no longer joined them for lunch. Rajesh had not told anyone about the captivity or what it had done to him. That was his secret, the thing he carried in silence, and it had become the thing that was slowly eroding his marriage, his job, and his sense of himself as a capable man. When Priya finally insisted that he see someone, that something was clearly very wrong, Rajesh had reluctantly agreed. He sat in that therapist's office now, exhausted and afraid, hoping that somehow, someone could help him reclaim the sense of safety that had been stolen from him thirty-two years ago. Because darkness itself had become a trigger-a return to that locked storage room-he flooded the bedroom with light and asked Priya again for reassurance, ran his hands over his skin checking for marks, performed the rituals that might keep the night from swallowing him whole.
